4396:
What if Bitcoin revolutionizes energy as much as it does money?

What if the impact of Bitcoin’s energy revolution was as positive to humanity as the impact of Bitcoin’s monetary revolution?

What if right under our noses Bitcoin’s impact on energy was already as big as Bitcoin’s impact on money?

When Satoshi created Bitcoin, he birthed not just a monetary revolution, but the twin revolutionary forces of a new approach to money and a new approach to energy.

While Bitcoin’s monetary revolution was by design, the energy revolution is by accident. For this reason, it often doesn’t get the same coverage and attention.

This accidental Bitcoin revolution is already showing signs of reshaping humanity in a way that has the potential to impact all of our lives.

In this article, I cover the five reasons why convergence between energy and Bitcoin mining is happening at pace.

Let’s get started:

As Lyn Alden points out, money is fundamentally broken. It turns out that energy is fundamentally broken too. Lyn Alden wrote a book on the first point.

First, some context on energy and grids:

Unlike the Internet, energy needs wires to transport. Lots of them.

Unlike a digital nomad using the Internet to live freely anywhere in the world, energy is a prisoner of time and space.

Energy cannot be effectively stored at scale (even with batteries) for more than four hours.

Energy cannot be efficiently transported either. Officially, transmission and distribution lose around 8% of the world’s electricity, but, like inflation, the real figure is much higher than the official figure.

Energy-generation also cannot be effectively coupled with the energy-use at the right time of day, leading to massive peaks and troughs in energy demand.

When old, centrally architected grids meet aggressive decarbonization and energy scale-up goals, we see five ways in which the systems we use to distribute energy are broken. Yes, Bitcoin fixes this, it’s already started fixing this, and it is happening at pace. Here’s how.


1. Centralized

Like financial systems, today's energy transmission and distribution systems are highly centralized. Grids are like the energy equivalent of a central bank: they are inefficient at getting resources to people who need it equitably. Micro-grids (small local grids) are the solution. But historically, the challenge has been that with a smaller population being served, the statistical chance of power being generated at a time people don’t need it is even higher.

How Bitcoin accelerates development of decentralized energy systems

Bitcoin solves this problem, because when people don’t need power, you simply mine Bitcoin. That pays off the micro-grid faster while lowering the cost of power to micro-grid users.

This beneficial impact is not theory. It is exactly what Gridless has already shown is possible in rural Africa, where its mining sites had brought power to 8,000 homes in Kenya, Malawi and Zambia by 2024.

Having proven this works in theory and in practice, there is now no barrier to scaling the renewable-microgrid/Bitcoin mining hybrid solution throughout Africa. Ultimately this isn’t just a solution for Africa, decentralization could in decades to come be the global way that energy is delivered. It would be both possible and poetic that a decentralized monetary system were the catalyst for the decentralization of energy systems.

2. Subsidized

Solar is a cool technology. What's more intuitively appealing than capturing the abundant energy of the sun! It's efficient, renewable, zero marginal cost power.

But have government subsidies for solar worked? There's a litany of examples of where Government solar subsidies have led to heavily under-used, unwanted, untransportable, or even obsolescent solar farms. This has happened across the world, including the EU, Northern Territory Australia, Spain, Texas, China, India, South Africa, Chile and Finland. Aside from the wasted energy, more than 2,750 GW of renewable energy is stuck in interconnection queues (waiting lists to connect to the grid) in just 10 jurisdictions, led by the US, the EU and India. Even counting only projects at advanced stages of development, the IEA (International Energy Agency) finds 1,500 GW of renewable projects waiting to connect worldwide.

How Bitcoin offers governments a subsidy-free future, while fixing the problems that existing subsidies created


Bitcoin mining fixes each case mentioned above. It does this by buying up wasted/ stranded solar energy that got overbuilt in the wrong places due to government subsidies. Bitcoin mining also helps politicians by making short-sighted political decisions around subsidies look smart after the fact.

Nowhere is this more apparent than in Texas.

Texas got solar subsidies through Federal tax credits (e.g. Roserock Solar Farm, 328 MW).

Before Bitcoin mining came onto Texas’ ERCOT (Electric Reliability Council of Texas) grid, solar and wind farms were under-utilized due to

1. Grid Constraints: Congestion in West Texas limits solar export to cities like Dallas

2. Curtailment (cutting the output of solar or wind farms when the grid can’t take their power): Solar farms in the Permian Basin compete with wind and fossil fuels, leading to wasted energy during low-price periods

3. Market Volatility: Subsidies encouraged overbuilding, but falling power prices reduce profitability

Because of this underutilization, pressure mounted to stop producing more wasteful solar (and wind farms). But in 2021, Bitcoin mining companies entered onto the grid and started buying the solar and wind energy that no-one else wanted. Sometimes they co-located on the solar or wind farm. At other times they provided a buyer for that otherwise wasted renewable energy. Then they helped counterbalance their intermittency once on the grid. These three factors helped solar and wind farm generators lift their generation capacity on ERCOT’s grid from 33.6 GW in September 2021 to 80.5 GW in July 2026.

Meanwhile, Brad Jones, ERCOT’s former interim CEO, has said that 3 GW of flexible Bitcoin mining demand was part of what enabled that expansion. Peer-reviewed research shows why. Lal and You found that Texas had more to gain than any other US state: 32 planned renewable projects in Texas could earn combined profits of $47 million by mining Bitcoin before they began commercial operation. A second peer-reviewed study, in Heliyon, showed that a 50MW solar farm would normally take 8.1 years to become profitable, but using Bitcoin mining it could reduce this to a mere 3.5 year payback. Like all responsible business owners, the solar generator would use profits to expand their operation.

3. Politicized

Today, what does the political left care more about?

  • environmental security (and to an extent energy equity)

What does the political right care more about?

  • energy security

It didn’t use to be this way. In the 1980s, Conservative Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher spoke actively about climate change and stated the UK must move beyond coal. By contrast, on the political left, prominent figures in the British Labour Party including both leader Neil Kinnock and former leader Michael Foot argued that coal was a vital source of jobs, vital to the economy, and vital to UK’s energy security following the 1973 oil crisis.

So while these alignments are tribal, which tribe aligns with which set of arguments can and has changed radically over time.

I recently wrote about how the decarbonization policies of today’s left and the energy security policies of today’s right have been implemented in a foolish way.

Until we look for solutions that combine the best of what the left and right want, we will continue to yo-yo between the decarbonization goals of the left and the energy security goals of the right. Ultimately, both will fail to adequately deliver either goal.

How Bitcoin is a non-partisan tool for decarbonization and energy security


Without a tool, the paragraph above that you just read is just ideological hope. Bitcoin is the tool that turns the statement from ideological hope to implementable reality.

Bitcoin increases energy security by making local sources of power generation more profitable. But Bitcoin also allows us to profitably decarbonize at the same time, in ways which include:

  • accelerating the renewable energy transition (Lal et al, 2023)
  • obviating the need for carbon-intensive gas peaker plants (Bruno et al, 2023)
  • stabilizing the grid while it scales to handle more renewables (Rudd et al, 2023)
  • halving the payback time for solar farms (Hakimi et al, 2024)
  • accelerating renewable microgrid development (Moghimi et al 2024)
  • reducing methane emissions from landfills (Sechrest et al, 2024)

These are not ideal theoretical possibilities, these benefits exist right now. I've documented the numerous case studies where they’re occurring in this longer article.

4. Fossilized

By fossilized, I don’t mean fossil-fuel based grids, I mean grids that are really old.

How bad is the situation? Well, imagine there’s no wireless cell phone network and all communication must be done over a wired landline phone network that hasn’t been maintained or upgraded for 30 years: that’s our modern energy infrastructure. It’s fossilized, under-maintained and in no position to handle additional load, or additional variable renewable energy (VRE) generation

That’s the state of grids in much of the world. In advanced economies, more than half of grid infrastructure is over 20 years old, according to the IEA.

But does this have an impact? The short answer is “yes.” It fundamentally impacts how much new VRE can be placed on them, a phenomenon that has been widely covered in mainstream media.

Many grids are struggling to meet today’s capacity, let alone the much harder future demands placed on grids by the more constant load balancing (matching power use to the power available) needed when you have high concentrations of VRE – aka Solar and Wind – on them.

How Bitcoin proves an almost cost-neutral fix to the issue of aging grids

Bitcoin mining has been shown to largely, if not completely, remedy the issue (Norris et al, 2025) of load balancing new VRE, avoiding the expensive grid-upgrade costs that would otherwise be incurred in order to handle more intermittency. In short, Bitcoin mining is a hack that means you can put more VRE onto even an aging grid, without astronomical upgrade costs. In fact, it’s the only way you can put more VRE onto an aging grid without astronomical upgrade costs.

5. Wasteful

On the grid, wasted energy is normally renewable energy: either it’s solar or wind produced at a time of day when people don’t want it, or a part of the country where people aren’t around to use it. Then there is hydro, which in the rainy season of many nations, including Norway, New Zealand, China and Costa Rica, simply flows over the top of the dam on a seasonal basis.

While batteries and pumped hydro are part of the solution, they are not the whole solution. Batteries will only store for 4 hours (not much use if you have surplus wind during a storm for 96 hours). And due to topographical issues, pumped hydro is only a solution for a small subset of hydro-dams.

What this means is, without a flexible user of energy, all this renewable power will continue to be squandered. For example in the UK, Scottish Wind farms now waste 20% of their energy.

What is the cost of this? Enormous. One site, Wastedwind.energy quantifies how much wind energy alone the UK wastes on a daily basis. Just 78 days into 2025: $417 Million of wasted power.

How Bitcoin prevents the wasting of renewable energy

Pavel Grachev calculates that Bitcoin could not have stopped the expense of needing to fire up gas plants. But, he calculates, had wind farms been used for Bitcoin mining rather than curtailed, it would have turned a $70.6 Million curtailment cost to the grid into a $91.5 Million Bitcoin mining revenue opportunity. Plus, by dealing with renewable intermittency at the front end of the queue, there could be even more renewable energy on the grid, which would have further reduced expenses by meaning fewer gas plants were called upon.

As we saw in the section on subsidies, this is not a fantasy: since 2021, Bitcoin mining companies helped catalyze an extra 47 GW of wind and solar capacity on ERCOT’s grid alone.

Summary

As we can see, the areas where Bitcoin mining is solving major systemic issues with the grid are both wide and deep. Both peer-reviewed research and real-life case studies have showcased how Bitcoin is able to overcome the challenges of our current energy system which is centralized, subsidized, politicized, fossilized and wasteful.

These are the five reasons that the energy sector needs Bitcoin mining. There are also economic drivers that mean Bitcoin mining companies need to become energy companies. Together, these pull and push factors are the reasons that convergence of Bitcoin mining and energy are happening rapidly.

“The wise do not desire to do anything’ and the wise do not desire to abandon action either” ~ Yoga Vasistha

This article was first published in The Bitcoin Adoption Letter in March 2025.
4397:
Here we tackle a topical question: what will happen to the world under two different scenarios: grids packed with Bitcoin mining vs grids packed with AI data centers?

First some context: right now, Bitcoin mining and AI data centers are in a power struggle for power on the grid. Basically there’s not enough power and too many users wanting that power, especially in the US, where the grid has not increased its generation capacity since 2007: that’s 17 years!

So two tribes; limited resources. Sounds like a recipe for tension right? Let’s find out.

First let’s understand each tribe. The key difference between Bitcoin mining and AI/HPC data centers is in their energy consumption patterns. Bitcoin mining can ramp up or throttle down its energy usage on a dime. This flexibility makes them perfect for balancing out the fluctuating energy supply from renewables.

On the other hand, AI data centers need 24/7 uptime. This means they're not as adaptable to the ebbs and flows of renewable energy.

So while AI data centers are busy crunching numbers and trying to figure out why we humans are so weird, Bitcoin miners are out there, flexing their energy consumption muscles and helping to stabilize the grid.

However, as this graphic from a whitepaper by Rhodes et al shows, flexible data centers like Bitcoin mining operations help grid operators to decarbonize grids, while inflexible data centers mean grid operators must build more fossil-fuel baseload onto the grid to meet their 24/7 requirements.

The authors were independent energy experts from outside the Bitcoin ecosystem, and the paper they wrote is probably the most important paper ever written about Bitcoin and its impact on grids, because the repercussions are so huge.

Extrapolating Rhodes’ findings into the future, it’s no stretch to say that whether it’s more Bitcoin mining, or more AI on the grid could determine whether grids meet their net zero emission targets.

It’s a little known secret that Bitcoin data centers are the world’s most flexible data centers.

So next time you hear someone verbally copy&paste some journalist’s latest piece of Bitcoin gaslighting, ask them how they feel about AI data centers.

Any way you cut it, if your goal is net zero emissions, Bitcoin mining moves us closer to that target, whereas AI data centers move us further away from it.

I cover AI and Bitcoin mining in more depth in my keynote at the MadBitcoin Summit 2026.

This article was first published in The Bitcoin Adoption Letter in June 2024.
4415:
This is not a story of terahash and megawatts. It’s the story about Eduardo. A man living less than an hour from me, on the jungle-clad side of the Poás volcano in land his family had owned for 5 generations in Alajuela province of Costa Rica. 

Many years ago, he’d had the smart idea to build a renewable microhydro station, to use the untapped power of the river that ran down the side of the volcano. 

The project was successful, but capital intensive. He took out a loan to pay for the investment, and life was good. For many years he sold the power back to the grid, earning a steady profit each year. 

Then COVID hit.

As businesses shut down, so did the demand for power. Without warning, ICE, the country’s state-owned energy utility, contacted him with the message: “We are permanently ending our power purchase agreements with all private electricity generators, effective immediately.” 

Half of a million dollars per year gone overnight. What would you do?

Overnight, a profitable business was turned into a debt burden. Eduardo valiantly attempted to transform the property into an eco-tourism destination. This brought in a little money, but nowhere near enough to pay his monthly bank interest repayments. 

After months of rising debt, he went to the bank and placed the keys to the property on his bank manager’s desk. He said, “I cannot repay this loan, and I am forfeiting the property, the hydro station and the dwellings to you.”

His bank manager was shocked. “What am I going to do with a micro-hydrostation?” he said. “Look just hold your horses for 6 months, let’s wait and see.” 

Eduardo shrewdly replied, “I can hold my horses, if you can hold your interest.”

They talked, and a mortgage holiday was arranged. 

But this was only a stay of execution. 

One day, 3 months later, with still no prospect of paying off his debt, Eduardo was talking to his son-in-law. “Have you considered Bitcoin?” He said.

Eduardo’s reaction was the same as mine when I first heard of Bitcoin. “What, that Ponzi scheme? Forget it!” But his son-in-law persisted. “Bitcoin miners need a lot of energy, and they can locate anywhere” he said. 

A lightbulb went off in Eduardo’s head.

Within days, he had bought a second hand S19 miner (a latest model mining rig at the time) and hooked it up to the power. Immediately he was earning Bitcoin. Days later, he was sitting in a café eating a meal he’d paid for with the Bitcoin he’d mined. He ran some calculations, and realized he’d found the answer. 

His bank manager did not share his enthusiasm for the answer.

Due to Costa Rica having strong user adoption for Bitcoin, banks had already seen a loss of business to Bitcoin as people preferred self-custodial wallets (where people hold their own Bitcoin rather than leaving it with a company) to bank savings accounts, and Lightning (Bitcoin’s fast payments network) to bank wire transfers. 

“We are not allowed to get involved with anything with the name Bitcoin in it,” his manager replied. “But if you call it a data center, I can give you a loan.” 

Three years later, I visited Eduardo’s 60 Ha property and mining operation. To describe it as paradise is no exaggeration. He employs 40 people for his ecotourism business. Hiking trails and zip lines traverse through the jungle. Free-range animals roam the property. Migratory birds stop to chill on his water reservoir as they fly south. Free-range geese and donkeys roam the property. The land is organic, grows its own food, and sees parties of visitors from schools to executive retreats pass through every week. 

He has become an avid supporter of Bitcoin, runs his own node and organizes local meetups to explain the value of Bitcoin to the community. 

“Where would you be without Bitcoin mining?” I asked him. He looked wistfully at the property and said - the hydro plant would be rusting. There would be no staff. And I would have lost this property of 5 generations to the bank. 

Eduardo’s story is not an anomaly. As Eduardo said to me, “Everything is energy”. Everything we see that looks solid is in fact just energy. The only choice we have is do we waste that energy or do we channel it into doing something that benefits people.

Whether it is hydro energy in Costa Rica, microgrid energy in a village in Africa, heat recycling in Finland, bathhouse heating in New York, grid balancing in Texas, or biogas from a landfill in Utah, or a pig farm in Ireland, Bitcoin mining companies are turning wasted power into flourishing energy distribution ecosystems that benefit humanity. 

Troy Cross once shared with me, “Normally you just get to watch history, but we are all creating it.”

On the night that Bill Maher tweeted the biggest “Bitcoin is bad for the environment” throwback I’ve seen on Twitter this year, complete with a 16x overestimation of Bitcoin’s energy consumption, it’s good to remember that for every Bill, there are many more Eduardos, quietly getting on with changing the world for the better. You won’t read about them in the media.

For more on how Bitcoin mining can cut emissions, see how Bitcoin mining could go carbon negative.

This article was first published in The Bitcoin Adoption Letter in October 2024.
4416:
In an earlier report we saw how 329,000 refugees had used Bitcoin to set up their lives in a new country.

After that was released, I got a message from a stranger saying “Thank you so much for your report. I’m one of them.” I asked if he would like his story to be shared here and he generously agreed. Warning: what follows is the incredible, sometimes heart-wrenching, story of how “the other half lives” in ways we can barely begin to imagine, and how Bitcoin is making a real difference to their lives.

Imagine waking up one Saturday morning to find that the money you’ve saved for decades is worthless. Not worth less, actually worthless - because the government decreed without warning you that it was no longer legal tender.

No problem, I still have my money in the bank right? No. This is Burma in 1987. The banking system is virtually non-existent. You have your savings in pieces of paper currency, stored securely in your home. Now those pieces of paper are literally just pieces of paper.

That nightmare became a reality for many in Myanmar (Burma) on September 5, 1987. Out of the blue, Ne Win, the country’s military-backed ruler, demonetized the 25, 35 and 75 kyat notes (that is, made them worthless by decree overnight).

The move made some 75% of the country’s currency worthless. In an era when banks were seldom used for saving, many Burmese citizens saw their life savings evaporate overnight. Of course, if you were an insider with close ties to the ruling military, you would have received a tip-off and already converted your Burmese cash into hard assets like gold and real estate.

This demonetization laid the foundation for decades of economic instability. In the case of Win Ko Ko Aung, born six years later, it meant he was born into poverty. That was a direct result of the ruling government’s control of the monetary system (a power that democratic governments also have, but most people trust them not to use).

Despite growing up in the central commercial city of Yangon and gaining early exposure to the Internet, his life was defined by control. Electricity was intermittent, and the government held a monopoly over telecommunications. Internet access was prohibitively expensive and restricted, with the regime actively spreading propaganda that discouraged youth use.

Hope arrived in 2011 with the transition to a democratic government, followed by the historic visit of President Barack Obama the next year. Inspired by the changing landscape and the influx of multinational companies that ensued, Aung decided to forgo the path of many peers, moving to countries like Singapore or Korea for more stable currency income. However, he ended up participating in the nation’s democratic revolution.

In 2018, he was selected as the Southeast Asia Youth Leader and got an opportunity to travel to the USA for a 3-month fellowship. Once there, he taught Internet and digital literacy to African American kids in South Chicago.

Coming back from the USA inspired, he established a successful digital technology company promoting literacy across the country. He was making an impact in society while earning a good income. However, he couldn’t see a great financial future against the backdrop of currency devaluation. As he recounts:

“I was making money, not in USD or in Singapore dollar, but in Myanmar Kyat, which is like melting ice cubes. I was making money, but mathematically speaking, I was never going to be able to buy a house, unless I would make a 100% increase in income, year after year.”

To preserve his wealth, he initially explored gold (too inconvenient to redeem) and savings in USD in a bank account. Though he had previously dismissed Bitcoin in 2015 and 2017 after encountering negative mainstream media coverage, his desperate need for a stable financial solution compelled him to investigate decentralized digital assets. He eventually invested a portion of his savings across Bitcoin and other digital assets.

The digital silencing of dissent

On February 1 2021, government intervention changed the trajectory of Aung’s life for a second time. The Burmese military staged a coup, erasing a decade of democratic progress. Aung, now a social entrepreneur with over 500,000 followers on his Facebook page, was one of the leaders in the decentralized democracy movement. He used his following to marshal followers to protest the military takeover.

The military junta weaponized the centralized financial system to exert control over Aung and others. Aung awoke one day to find he had been locked out of his bank account, losing all his USD savings.

Happily, his Bitcoin and other digital assets remained safe because the government couldn’t gain access.

Other major voices in the movement faced similar lockouts or outright arrest. Supporters who donated $8 or less to the pro-democracy movement were sentenced to seven to ten years in jail.

By April 2021, Aung was on the country’s Most Wanted List. Fearing for his life, he fled, crossing the border into Thailand and seeking refuge. He was later granted asylum and resettled in the United States, where his advocacy continued. However, an interview with Voice of America, conducted in the Burmese language, alerted the military to his continued activism via his Facebook platform.

The regime responded by arresting his elderly mother. Her freedom was eventually negotiated on two explicit conditions: that Aung cease his advocacy activities and, most critically, that he delete his Facebook account. Fearing for his mother’s safety, he abided - losing all 500,000 followers instantly. This silenced his primary digital platform. It was an illustration of the authoritarian playbook: weaponizing financial and family ties to suppress dissent.

A tool for human rights advancement

In the US, Aung secured menial jobs but simultaneously deepened his understanding of Bitcoin. He later joined the Human Rights Foundation, shifting his focus to international human rights and Bitcoin advocacy, which he has done since.

Today, Aung is one of the hundreds of thousands of refugees who have been able to use Bitcoin to preserve and transport wealth during crises. He notes:

“I support Bitcoin, especially for activists and democracy movements, because with other cryptocurrencies, you need to constantly worry. There are a lot of risks. You’ll be worried about what their marketing team is going to do, what the founder is going to do. A lot of political influence also impacts the assets, and governments can block transactions to activists.”

To him, Bitcoin represents freedom, particularly for those under oppressive regimes. Its uncensorable nature makes it uniquely suited for activists and decentralized movements, allowing for support and communication that cannot be easily blocked or seized by state authorities.

More importantly, his journey led him to a crucial realization. Stablecoins (digital tokens pegged to a currency such as the US dollar) also offered a way to preserve value. But Bitcoin’s true decentralization means it has no single founder or central entity that governments can identify and compel to enforce their will. That is a significant advantage over other digital assets.

Having personally experienced the effects of monetary collapse, real-time asset demonetization, and the total loss of all personal savings, Aung’s trust in Bitcoin is born out of experience and necessity, not ideology. Furthermore, his firsthand experience of starting a new life in a new country was immediately supported by Bitcoin donated by fellow advocates, empowering him to get on his feet faster. The stories of people like Aung show us that Bitcoin is much more than an investment - it is a tool for human progression, a bulwark against authoritarian control.

So the next time you hear someone say “Bitcoin has no use” - know that what they are actually saying, whether knowingly or unknowingly, is “The lives of people like Aung don’t matter.” The viewpoint is not progressive, it is reactionary: born out of either prejudice, ignorance, or a failure to extend either their imagination or their cognitive bandwidth outside of their Western bubble of comfort and privilege.

Don’t get angry with such people, after all I used to be that ignorant person myself. Rather, educate them with stories like this one that show the gaps in their perception.

This article was first published in The Bitcoin Adoption Letter in September 2025.
4417:
The city-camp

Imagine a city 50 miles from the Kenya/Somalia border of over 420,000 people (about the size of Minneapolis), a city on no tourist maps, where homes are huts of sticks and cloth, and the struggle for daily survival is a universal reality. This is the Dadaab refugee camp in Kenya, one of the largest in the world, established in 1991 when refugees started fleeing across the Kenyan border during Somalia’s civil war.

For many, like Fatuma who arrived after her husband was killed in an explosion in Mogadishu, Dadaab is a last resort. She now lives with her family in a makeshift hut on the camp's outskirts, a structure patched together from branches and old clothes, where they sleep on dirt and pray the roof doesn't collapse when it rains.

Others, like Saruro (pictured below), have known no other home. She arrived in 1992 as a three-year-old and has since built an entire life here, going to school, getting married, and raising her nine children within the camp's confines. Many residents have spent decades here, with over half of the Somali refugees being under 18 and having spent their entire lives in Dadaab.

Life can be particularly hard if you are a woman. Women live in fear of rape, particularly when venturing out to find basic resources like firewood.

Theft and armed robberies are daily facts of life, with thieves often acting with impunity due to a lack of policing. In response, many refugees have become their own guardians. They organize night patrols, lock gates between camp subdivisions after dark, and use watchmen armed with machetes, sticks, and stones to defend against attackers who often carry AK-47s. As Wiilo Ibrahim (pictured below) explains “We are afraid of thieves. They rob houses, and girls are raped. It is trouble … at night, you have to be on alert.”

Ingenuity

Despite these challenges, human ingenuity survives, and sometimes thrives. While earning money is extremely difficult, it is not impossible. Some, like Hawo Mohamed Abdi, a 29-year-old single mother, have found a lifeline through the digital economy. After taking online business courses, she now works as a translator from her hut in the camp, earning $500 a month, enough to achieve independence and renovate her hut.

Others, like Abdullahi Abdirahman Nur, use similar skills to support his family of eight, even saving enough to relocate his parents to a safer town. However, these stories are the outliers. Most residents rely on dwindling humanitarian aid, and storing money safely is a constant worry in an environment where theft is rampant.

Dadaab is a world of contradictions. It is a temporary refuge camp, that has lasted generations. It is a place where women like Fardowsa (pictured below) a journalist born in the camp, now work to amplify the voices of those within it. It is a camp, but also a city for those who have nowhere else to go.

Aisha

One of those contradictions is Aisha (not her real name). A refugee from the camp who unintentionally showed Bryon Bothun, a former American Peace Corps worker, the value of Bitcoin - even though she never had the chance to own it herself.

Bryon and his wife Christine met in the PeaceCorps in 1989. Bryon and Christine are now retired, but at the time this story takes place Christine was an occupational therapist working with children with autism, and Bryon was the Director of Bilingual Services in Rochester Public Schools. In his job he helped refugees from over 80 countries, drawing on his own experience being an outsider. He says, “I look around the room and I see the one person who’s different.”

Married with two adult children, the Bothuns continue to live the lessons they learned abroad: that community requires no words, and that sometimes those who have the least, give the most.

This was certainly the case, when Aisha changed the direction of Bryon’s life.

The lightbulb moment

Bryon recalls “We had invited Aisha over one afternoon, and by accident we found ourselves watching Max Keiser when he was first talking about Bitcoin. I was skeptical and spoke my thoughts aloud, saying to Aisha “I don’t see how that could help at all”. Her response caused me to take note. She said “We would have loved to have had that in Dadaab.”

Intrigued, I asked her to tell me more. She explained “You couldn’t keep money. People would come into your hut and they would take it from you. But people had a cellphone and they guarded it with their life, and they overpaid their bill to Safaricom and those credits became M-Pesa.” She said

“If we could have had money that wasn’t dependent on us paying our money to Safaricom each month, every single person in that refugee camp would’ve had it.”

That was the first time that I thought, “I hadn’t thought of that, maybe there is something to this.”

She turned on the lights for me, and it’s really thanks to her that I first saw the value of Bitcoin, started using it and started educating others about the value of it.”

Since Aisha’s experience, over 300,000 refugees now use Bitcoin - a figure that could have been much higher with better education and understanding of what Bitcoin is. More aid workers knowing about Bitcoin means more thefts can be prevented. The good news is that refugee use of Bitcoin is projected to grow to between 6.5 and 7.5 million by 2035.

How you can help

Bitcoin isn't a company, it's a tool for people. It offers returns to a Wall Street fund manager, but safety to a refugee. It has no CEO and no ads. Its value is shown in human stories, like Aisha's.

But without a PR team, these stories are rarely told. Most people only hear the jargon, not the hope. They'll understand Bitcoin best through simple stories like this one.

This article was first published in The Bitcoin Adoption Letter in November 2025.
